topic: the concept of a chemical formula unit for ionic compounds

easy.text: Ionic compounds like NaCl don't exist as individual molecules but rather as a repeating crystal lattice. What is the term for the simplest ratio of ions in such a compound?

options.feedback: Correct -- a formula unit represents the simplest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound's crystal structure.
The term 'molecule' technically applies to covalently bonded, discrete units -- ionic compounds use 'formula unit' instead, since they form extended lattices.
An atom is a single basic unit of an element, not the specific ratio-based unit used for ionic compounds.
Isotope refers to atoms of the same element with different neutron counts, unrelated to describing ionic compound ratios.

medium.text: Why is it inaccurate to refer to a 'molecule' of table salt (NaCl)?

options.text: NaCl exists as a continuous 3D crystal lattice of alternating ions, not as discrete, separate molecular units
options.feedback: Correct -- unlike covalent molecules (like H₂O), ionic compounds form extended repeating structures rather than individual bonded units.

options.text: NaCl doesn't actually contain any real chemical bonds
options.feedback: NaCl does contain real ionic bonds -- the issue is specifically about the extended lattice structure, not an absence of bonding altogether.

options.text: NaCl is actually a mixture, not a compound at all
options.feedback: NaCl is genuinely a chemical compound (with a fixed, bonded ratio of elements) -- it's just structured as a lattice rather than discrete molecules.

options.text: This terminology distinction doesn't actually matter in chemistry
options.feedback: This distinction (molecule vs. formula unit) is actually a meaningful and standard part of accurate chemical terminology.

hard.text: Since NaCl doesn't exist as discrete molecules, why do chemists still write its formula as "NaCl" (a 1:1 ratio) rather than describing the entire crystal structure?

options.text: The formula "NaCl" represents the simplest whole-number ratio of ions throughout the entire crystal, which is sufficient to describe the compound's composition without needing to describe every ion in the lattice
options.feedback: Correct -- since the ratio remains constant throughout the entire crystal (however large), this simplified formula unit efficiently and accurately represents the compound's overall composition.

options.text: The formula "NaCl" is actually incorrect and chemists have simply never bothered to fix it
options.feedback: This formula is actually correct and standard -- it properly represents the compound's fixed ionic ratio, which is all that's needed to describe its composition.

options.text: Every crystal of table salt contains exactly one sodium atom and one chlorine atom, nothing more
options.feedback: A real crystal contains an enormous number of ions -- the formula represents their RATIO (1:1), not a literal count of just two atoms total.

options.text: This formula only applies to a single, specific grain of salt and nothing larger
options.feedback: This formula ratio applies consistently to any amount of NaCl, from a single unit cell up to an entire visible crystal, not just one specific tiny grain.

easy.hard: This term describes the smallest repeating ratio representing an ionic compound's composition.
easy.medium: This term describes the simplest ratio of ions that make up the compound.
easy.easy: This is the name for the simplest ratio of ions in a compound like salt.

medium.hard: Consider the fundamental structural difference between discrete covalently-bonded units and an extended, repeating ionic lattice.
medium.medium: Salt is actually a huge repeating pattern of ions, not separate individual units like a water molecule.
medium.easy: Salt isn't made of separate little units -- it's one big repeating pattern of ions.

hard.hard: Since the ionic ratio remains invariant throughout the entire lattice regardless of crystal size, the simplified formula unit efficiently captures the compound's essential compositional information.
hard.medium: Since the same 1:1 ratio holds true no matter how big the crystal is, that simple ratio is really all you need to describe it.
hard.easy: Since the same 1-to-1 ratio holds true no matter how big the crystal is, that's really all you need to know.
